rules.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to Berkeley landlords a coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley. It is also unlawful for a landlord to use such an algorithm when setting rents or occupancy levels. rules.key_value: Unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a restraint of trade, or to coerce others to adopt its recommended price or commercial term
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
rules.requirement: It is unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce. It is also unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm if the person coerces another person to set or adopt the price or commercial term the algorithm recommends for the same or similar products or services in California. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including a computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. The section does not limit the antitrust laws. A companion section lets a Cartwright Act complaint proceed on plausible factual allegations of a contract, combination, or conspiracy, without alleging facts that exclude independent action.

coverage_conditions.text: Applies to housing providers statewide, including landlords, property managers and tenant screening companies. The page gives no unit-count, age-of-building or owner-type threshold for this rule.

rules.key_value: No blanket ban on applicants with a criminal history; convictions must be directly related to tenancy
rules.quoted_span: Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.
rules.requirement: Housing providers may check an applicant's criminal history, but they cannot consider arrests that did not lead to a conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile justice records. They cannot have blanket bans on all people with a criminal history. A denial based on a conviction must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant and not a threat to the health and safety of others or the property. Providers should weigh the nature and severity of the crime and the time since the conduct.
rules.title: California FEHA limits on using criminal history in tenant screening

parameters.text: Owns only two rental properties; ownership held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC where all members are natural persons

coverage_conditions.text: Applies to rental units generally. The two-month small-landlord allowance depends on owning only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total, held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC with only natural-person members.

exemptions: Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total may charge up to two months' rent, if ownership is held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC where all members are natural persons
rules.key_value: 1 month's rent cap; 2 months' rent for small landlords
rules.quoted_span: Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may only charge one month's rent for unfurnished and furnished units
rules.requirement: Starting July 1, 2024, most landlords may charge a security deposit of no more than one month's rent for furnished and unfurnished units. Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four units total may charge up to two months' rent if the owner is a natural person, family trust, or LLC whose members are all natural persons. The page also says a deposit balance must be returned within 21 days after the tenant leaves, with an itemized statement of any deductions.
rules.title: California security deposit cap (AB 12)

coverage_conditions.text: Applies to any security held by a landlord under a lease or rental agreement. This chunk states no building-level conditions.

rules.key_value: Security may not be called nonrefundable; bad-faith retention damages up to twice the security amount
rules.quoted_span: A lease or rental agreement shall not contain a provision characterizing any security as “nonrefundable.”
rules.requirement: A lease or rental agreement may not describe any security deposit as "nonrefundable." A landlord or successor in interest who claims or keeps a security deposit (or any part of it) in bad faith, or demands replacement security in bad faith, may owe statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, plus actual damages. The landlord or successor bears the burden of proving the amounts claimed were reasonable. A successor who receives any part of the security takes on the landlord's rights and duties for it. Claims may be brought in small claims court within its jurisdictional limit.
rules.title: California security deposit rules: nonrefundable-deposit ban and bad-faith damages

rules.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.
rules.requirement: For residential rental agreements, a landlord may not demand or receive security of more than one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent paid before initial occupancy. Landlords who are natural persons (or LLCs whose members are all natural persons) and own no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total may charge up to two months' rent, unless the prospective tenant is a service member. The landlord may claim only amounts reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning, and restoring or returning personal property. The landlord must offer an initial inspection, take photographs, and return the remaining security with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates.

Amounts depend on whether the tenant is an eligible or qualified tenant, how long they have lived in the unit, and household income. rules.quoted_span: It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.
rules.requirement: Landlords in the City of Los Angeles may not end a tenancy without just cause. At-fault reasons include failure to pay rent, uncured lease violations, nuisance or damage, illegal use, refusal to renew a similar agreement, and refusal of reasonable access. No-fault reasons include owner or family move-in, demolition, removal from the rental market, government order, and conversion to non-residential or affordable housing. No-fault evictions require relocation assistance. The JCO covers most residential properties not regulated by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO). It applies once the tenant has lived in the unit at least six months or the original lease has expired, whichever comes first.

rules.requirement: A landlord or tenant may end a tenancy at will with written notice of three months. For nonpayment of rent, the landlord may end the tenancy with fourteen days' written notice to quit. That notice must include the statutory notification about the tenant's right to pay within ten days. This section sets notice and procedure requirements. It does not require a stated cause for ending the tenancy.

coverage_conditions.text: Applies to tenants of residential premises who engaged in protected activity: legal action to enforce housing law, reporting code violations, or organizing or joining a tenants' union.

exemptions: A notice of termination for nonpayment of rent does not trigger the six-month presumption
rules.key_value: Damages of 1 to 3 months' rent or actual damages (whichever is greater) plus costs and attorney's fees; 6-month rebuttable presumption of reprisal
rules.quoted_span: The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not threaten or take reprisals against a residential tenant who enforces housing laws in a judicial or administrative action, reports a health, building or housing code violation to a board of health or to the landlord, or organizes or joins a tenants' union. A reprisal makes the landlord liable for damages of at least one and at most three months' rent, or the tenant's actual damages if greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. A notice of termination of tenancy, rent increase or substantial change in tenancy terms received within six months after the protected activity is presumed to be a reprisal. The landlord can rebut the presumption only by clear and convincing evidence of independent justification. Any lease or rental-agreement waiver of this protection is void.
rules.title: Reprisal against tenants for protected activity prohibited

rules.requirement: At or before the start of a residential tenancy, a lessor or the lessor's agent may require only the first month's rent, the last month's rent at the first month's rate, a security deposit of no more than one month's rent, and the cost of a key and lock. The deposit must be held in a separate interest-bearing bank account in Massachusetts, and the tenant must get a receipt and a signed statement of the premises' condition. The tenant is owed 5% yearly interest, or the lesser rate the bank paid. The lessor must return the deposit, less permitted deductions with an itemized list, within 30 days after the tenancy ends. A lessor who breaks these rules can forfeit the right to keep any of the deposit and owe triple damages.

rules.key_value: Unlawful to use or operate algorithmic rent-setting coordinators (violation of the NJ Antitrust Act)
rules.quoted_span: any person to perform a coordinating function
rules.requirement: It is unlawful, and a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, for a rental property owner (or its agent or subcontractor) to pay for or subscribe to a coordinator's services. It is also unlawful for a coordinator to facilitate an agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition, for two or more persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination, and for any person to perform a coordinating function. A coordinator is a person who operates algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that sets or recommends rental prices, material lease terms or occupancy levels using the competitively sensitive information of other owners. The Attorney General receives complaints and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact ordinances that conflict with the act.
rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act

rules.key_value: $50 maximum application fee, adjusted annually for CPI
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that is more than $50. The cap is adjusted each year by the Director of the Division of Consumer Affairs in proportion to the percent change in the regional Consumer Price Index, and only if that change is greater than zero. A landlord who violates the cap is liable for a penalty of up to $500 for a first offense, up to $750 for a second offense and up to $1,000 for each later offense. The amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.
rules.title: Residential rental application fee capped at $50

rules.requirement: New Jersey has no state law that establishes, governs or controls rents. Municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances. Under the Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law, newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinance for 30 years after construction of the building is completed. Rents subsidized by governmental funding may also be exempt.

rules.requirement: A landlord or rental agency may not refuse to rent or discriminate in renting housing on protected grounds. These include race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union and domestic partnership status, familial status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, disability, nationality, and source of lawful income. The law applies to all landlord-tenant relationships except the listed exemptions.

rules.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before a conditional offer; look-back limits of 6 years (first degree), 4 years (second or third degree), 1 year (fourth degree) after the offer
rules.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.
rules.requirement: A housing provider may not ask about an applicant's criminal record, orally or in writing, or put such questions on an application, until it has made a conditional offer. Before or after the offer, it may not evaluate arrests without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. After a conditional offer, it may consider only listed serious convictions within set look-back periods (6 years for first-degree, 4 years for second- or third-degree, 1 year for fourth-degree indictable offenses). It may withdraw an offer only after an individualized assessment and must give written reasons and a chance to appeal. Before accepting an application fee, it must disclose in writing whether criminal history is considered and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracy or rehabilitation. It may not require drug or alcohol tests. The Division on Civil Rights enforces the act with penalties of up to $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations.

rules.key_value: Return within 30 days of tenancy end; double damages if wrongfully withheld
rules.quoted_span:
Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security 
deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant
rules.requirement: A landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest earned less itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Interest on the deposit belongs to the tenant. The landlord must give written notice of where the deposit is held within 30 days of receipt and at each annual interest payment. A landlord who wrongfully withholds the deposit can be sued for double the amount withheld, plus court costs and attorney's fees.
rules.title: NJ Security Deposit Law: interest, notice and return within 30 days

The landlord is not required to collect a security deposit
rules.key_value: Maximum deposit 1.5x one month's rent; yearly increase capped at 10% of current deposit; deposit plus first month's rent capped at 2.5x monthly rent at lease start
rules.quoted_span: one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ). It can be less.
rules.requirement: A landlord who collects a security deposit may not collect more than one and one-half times one month's rent. Any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. A pet security deposit is allowed only if, combined with the regular deposit, it stays within the one-and-one-half-month cap. Prepaid funds held to secure future rent, including last month's rent, count as part of the deposit. At lease inception the landlord may not require more than two and one-half times the monthly rent in total (deposit plus first month's rent). Deposit money stays the tenant's property and is held in trust. It must be kept in an insured New Jersey bank or savings and loan in an interest-bearing account, with the fund and variable-rate options for landlords holding deposits for 10 or more units. The law applies to most residential rentals, including mobile homes.
rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law: deposit cap, increase limit and handling
